summary: Specifies the syntax and semantics of the URI scheme for the STUN protocol, so a STUN server can be named in a URI. This makes STUN servers easy to name in configuration and in other protocols.

eli5.summary: It gives a special web-style address format for helper servers that tell computers how the outside sees them.

questions: how to write a stun server uri
subtitle: The stun: and stuns: URI schemes for naming a STUN server in configuration.

tldr.problem: Endpoints and web applications such as WebRTC need to be told which STUN server to use, and an inconsistent syntax would lead to ambiguity and non-interoperable solutions.
tldr.mechanism: Two URI schemes, stun and stuns, name a STUN server with a host and an optional port. The stuns scheme is used when STUN runs over TLS-over-TCP.
tldr.outcome: A consistent way to describe, configure and exchange STUN server information. The schemes are meant only for NAT traversal environments, not the open Web.

today: RFC 7064 is a Proposed Standard. The metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why STUN Needs a URI
sections.content:
STUN is a tool for other protocols dealing with Network Address Translator (NAT) traversal. An endpoint can use it to learn the IP address and port a NAT allocated to it, to run connectivity checks between two endpoints, and as a keepalive to maintain NAT bindings. RFC 5389 defines the protocol itself.

With WebRTC, the RFC expects many endpoints and web applications to need to identify a STUN server. They must be configured with it, and an inconsistent syntax adds ambiguity and can cause non-interoperable solutions. The stun and stuns URI schemes give one consistent way to describe, configure and exchange the information identifying a STUN server.
sections.eli5: Programs need to be told where the helper server lives. Writing the address one agreed way means nobody gets confused.

sections.title: URI Syntax
sections.content:
The formal syntax is short: stunURI = scheme ":" host [ ":" port ], where the scheme is stun or stuns. The host and port productions come from RFC 3986.

Although those productions are defined as parts of the generic hierarchical URI, this does not make these schemes hierarchical. Developers MUST NOT use a generic hierarchical URI parser to parse a stun or stuns URI. The design notes explain that the URIs are opaque because they do not describe a hierarchical structure.
sections.eli5: The address is just the word stun, a colon, the server name and maybe a number. It is not built like a web page address, so do not read it like one.

sections.title: Semantics: Scheme, Host and Port
sections.content:
The URI designates a stand-alone STUN server or any Internet host performing the operations of one. STUN can run over UDP, TCP or TLS-over-TCP. The stuns scheme MUST be used when STUN runs over TLS-over-TCP (or in the future DTLS-over-UDP), and the stun scheme MUST be used otherwise.

The host is required and names the server. If a port is present it is the port the server listens on. If it is absent, the default is 3478 for both UDP and TCP, and 5349 for STUN over TLS. For the optional DNS discovery procedure in RFC 5389, stun implies UDP for the SRV lookup and stuns implies TCP.
sections.eli5: The first word tells whether the chat with the helper is plain or locked. If no door number is given, a standard one is used.

sections.title: Examples
sections.content:
The appendix shows three URIs, all using example.org as the host: stun:example.org, stuns:example.org and stun:example.org:8000. The last one overrides the default port with 8000.

The appendix also records a design choice. Reviewers suggested dropping the s suffix and using a parameter such as ;proto=tls, but the authors declined because the need for the parameter could not be sufficiently explained and supporting it would leave the specification incomplete. It would also have lost symmetry with the TURN URI.
sections.eli5: These are sample addresses showing the plain form, the locked form and one with a custom door number.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The schemes add no security issues beyond those in RFC 3986. A stun or stuns URI does not carry a username or password, but in environments like WebRTC those credentials will almost certainly be provisioned remotely at the same time as the URI. If they arrive in the clear, there is little or no benefit to using stuns.

So a STUN client MUST ensure that the username, password, stuns URI and any other security-relevant parameters are received with equivalent security before using the stuns URI. Receiving them over another TLS session can be enough if both sessions are similarly parameterized, for example with commensurate strength ciphersuites. The IANA section adds that the schemes are for very specific NAT traversal environments and should not be used on the open Web or Internet.
sections.eli5: A locked address is not worth much if the key was handed over in the open. Send the settings as safely as you plan to use the server.
